reconcile.note: Matthew Henry reads Paul's celibacy preference as suited to the church's contemporary distress, not a verdict that marriage itself is bad or Genesis wrong to bless it.

discrepancy.note: Ingersoll traces the Catholic exaltation of celibacy over marriage to Paul's teaching and condemns it as a stain on marriage and love.

quotes.text: The Cardinal takes the ground that marriage is a sacrament, and therefore indissoluble, and he also insists that celibacy is far better than marriage,—holier than a sacrament,—that marriage is not the highest state, but that "the state of virginity unto death is the highest condition of man and woman."
quotes.attr: Robert G. Ingersoll (d. 1899), The Christian Religion, pt. III (1881), on Genesis 2:18 and 1 Corinthians 7:1.

quotes.text: This church followed the teachings of St. Paul. It taught the uncleanness of marriage, and insisted that all children were conceived in sin.
quotes.attr: Robert G. Ingersoll (d. 1899), The Christian Religion, pt. III (1881), on 1 Corinthians 7:1.

quotes.text: Celibacy is the essence of vulgarity. It tries to put a stain upon motherhood, upon marriage, upon love—that is to say, upon all that is holiest in the human heart.
quotes.attr: Robert G. Ingersoll (d. 1899), The Christian Religion, pt. III (1881), on Genesis 2:18.

sides.snippet: It is not good that the man should be alone
sides.verseText: Yahweh God said, \"It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper suitable for him.\"

sides.snippet: Now concerning the things about which you wrote to me: it is good for a man not to touch a woman.
sides.verseText: Now concerning the things about which you wrote to me: it is good for a man not to touch a woman.
